universal_lens: Training load and injury incidence are coupled through exposure-normalized event rates and multivariate inertial-sensor features, forming a volume-intensity state space whose trajectories predict non-contact soft-tissue injury risk while accounting for positional heterogeneity and session-type exposure differences.
gsi_mapping: Bayesian hierarchical models pool single-team evidence with league priors; posterior distributions over injury incidence are updated from athlete-exposure counts and sensor-derived load kernels, while conformal prediction sets quantify uncertainty for volume-intensity thresholds and positional strata, enabling decision-theoretic workload interventions.
gse_mapping: Each session is a state transition in a partially-observed Markov decision process; volume and intensity features drive transition probabilities to healthy, fatigued, and injured states, with game and practice contexts as distinct action spaces. Positional roles modulate the transition dynamics and available observations.

primitives.name: Athlete Exposure Injury Incidence Rate
primitives.verbatim_quote: Over a 16-year period, Hootman and colleagues(24) observed the risk of injury in American college football to be 9.6 injuries per 1000 athlete practice exposures and 35.9 injuries per 1000 athlete game exposures.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: I: number of injuries, dimensionless count; E_p: athlete practice exposures, dimensionless count; E_g: athlete game exposures, dimensionless count; R_p = (I/E_p) × 1000, injuries per 1000 practice exposures; R_g = (I/E_g) × 1000, injuries per 1000 game exposures.
primitives.assumptions: Injuries and exposures are consistently recorded across the 16-year surveillance period; practice and game exposures are mutually exclusive and standardized; all injury types are aggregated; athlete-exposure definition follows NCAA surveillance protocol.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Underreporting of minor injuries; variation in exposure-time definitions; low-frequency rare events; denominator misclassification between full and partial participation.

layer2.mapping: Maps to GSE state-transition hazard from healthy to injured under game/practice actions; in GSI it is a Poisson/Gamma Bayesian rate parameter with conjugate updating from exposure counts.
layer2.telemetry: Observed injury counts and athlete-exposure denominators by session type.

primitives.name: Player Load Volume Proxy
primitives.verbatim_quote: However, one limitation of this study was that only one inertial sensor variable, Player Load, was utilized in the investigation.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: PL: Player Load, arbitrary inertial-sensor units (a.u.); d: running distance, m; ρ: Pearson correlation coefficient between PL and d, dimensionless; t: time, s.
primitives.assumptions: Player Load is a monotonic proxy for total movement volume; single tri-axial accelerometer placement is consistent; correlation with running distance is stable across positions and sessions.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Saturation at high accelerations; insensitivity to high-intensity explosive actions; sensor drift or placement variation; non-linear volume-fatigue relationship.

layer2.mapping: In GSE it is a cumulative state variable driving volume transitions; in GSI it serves as a one-dimensional kernel feature whose marginal posterior informs workload priors.
layer2.telemetry: Catapult-derived Player Load per minute and per session.

primitives.name: Multivariate Inertial Sensor Training Load
primitives.verbatim_quote: Therefore, it is possible that other inertial sensor variables or a combination of inertial sensor variables may provide greater detail regarding injury risk because they quantify different aspects of the players' movement demands.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: L ∈ ℝⁿ: load vector of n inertial sensor variables; IMA_low: count of accelerations in 1.5–2.5 m·s⁻², dimensionless; IMA_med: count in 2.5–3.5 m·s⁻², dimensionless; IMA_high: count >3.5 m·s⁻², dimensionless; ImpactsLow/Med/High: counts of collisions in 5–6 g, 6–7 g, >7 g, dimensionless; g: gravitational acceleration, 9.80665 m·s⁻².
primitives.assumptions: Each sensor variable captures a distinct volume or intensity component; thresholds are fixed and physiologically meaningful; counts are additive across a session; positional differences are handled by stratification.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Multicollinearity among load components; threshold misalignment with individual capacity; double-counting of accelerative and impact events; band saturation.

layer2.mapping: Isomorphic to a multi-feature state vector in GSE; in GSI it becomes a multivariate Bayesian predictor with conformal uncertainty sets for injury risk conditioned on load profile and position.
layer2.telemetry: Per-session per-player counts for each IMA and Impact band.

primitives.name: Longitudinal Training Injury Cohort Window
primitives.verbatim_quote: The study period consisted of 24 weeks of training from the pre-season, regular season, and playoff periods for one NFL team.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: T: study duration, 24 weeks; N_s: number of training sessions, 76, dimensionless; t: calendar time, weeks; P: number of players, dimensionless.
primitives.assumptions: Single-team cohort is representative of NFL training; training sessions are the primary exposure unit; pre-season, regular season, and playoff periods are comparable; injury coding follows UEFA consensus recommendations.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Single-team external validity collapse; schedule-induced confounding; playoff selection bias; missing data from injured players; temporal non-stationarity of the load-injury relationship.

layer2.mapping: In GSE it defines a temporally extended episode with phase transitions (pre-season, regular, playoff); in GSI it supplies the longitudinal likelihood for hierarchical time-to-event models.
layer2.telemetry: Session-level training load and weekly injury status over 24 weeks.

reasoning_traces.think:
The operators are built from three core constructions. First, the exposure-normalized injury rate R = I/E × 1000 converts raw counts into an interpretable epidemiological signal, with separate rates for practice and game contexts. Second, Player Load PL is treated as a cumulative volume proxy, ideally proportional to integrated accelerometer magnitude and correlated with running distance. Third, the multivariate load vector L = [PL, IMA_low, IMA_med, IMA_high, ImpactsLow, ImpactsMed, ImpactsHigh] decomposes session demand into volume and intensity channels. The central duality is volume versus intensity: PL accumulates total mechanical work, while IMA and Impact bands count threshold exceedances that stress soft-tissue and collision systems. A plausible injury hazard takes the form h(L, position) = f(β₀ + β·L + γ(position)), where collinearity in L is the primary structural risk. Failure modes follow from measurement, model, and causal layers. Player Load misses high-intensity actions; IMA and Impact bands are discretized and may saturate. Positional baselines differ, so unstratified inference suffers distribution shift. Injury coding by staff introduces observer-dependent censoring, and the single-team design limits external validity. Autocorrelation across sessions violates independence, and contact injuries can leak into non-contact labels. The 24-week window mixes pre-season, regular-season, and playoff phases with non-stationary schedules. In GSE terms, the state space is partially observed because fatigue and tissue state are latent; in GSI terms, the likelihood is overdispersed and requires hierarchical regularization. Conformal or Bayesian credible sets must therefore accompany any threshold-based workload rule.

reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: Injury epidemiology in American football descends from NCAA surveillance (Hootman et al.) and the NCAA Injury Surveillance System, which standardized athlete-exposures. Wearable load metrics grew from accelerometer studies in Australian football and rugby, producing Player Load and IMA bands. Survival and count models (Poisson, negative binomial) were imported from biostatistics. Recent load-injury research merged these threads into multivariate training-load modeling.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: Sports scientists design load vectors, physiotherapists code injuries, coaches adjust practice schedules, and athletes may conceal fatigue or minor complaints; each actor holds private information and divergent incentives. League schedulers impose external constraints unrelated to team physiology. Consequently, the injury database is co-produced and strategically filtered, so the observed data distribution reflects institutional preferences, reporting thresholds, and competitive secrecy as much as biological mechanisms.
